title: Circuit breakers, bulkheads and hedging
summary: A circuit breaker stops calls to a failing dependency, a bulkhead stops one consumer from sinking the rest, and hedging sends an early duplicate to cut tail latency. Each trades capacity, cost or complexity for isolation or speed.
useIf: A failing or slow dependency, or one noisy consumer, can drag down everything else.
avoidIf: Traffic is small and failures are rare: simple retries and good timeouts are enough.

explain.md: A **circuit breaker** has three states. In **closed** it passes calls and counts recent failures. When failures exceed a threshold it moves to **open** and rejects calls quickly. After a trip period it enters **half-open**, lets a few calls through and closes again only if they succeed [[tr4]]. In API Management a backend has one `circuitBreaker` rule with `failureCondition`, `tripDuration` and `acceptRetryAfter`; a tripped breaker returns 503, rules are approximate across gateway instances, and the Consumption tier lacks them. For Azure OpenAI backends accept `Retry-After`, which can be very long [[r4]]. AWS warns breakers add modal behaviour that is hard to test and can slow recovery, so pair them with a local token bucket on retries [[tr3]].

A **bulkhead** partitions capacity into pools so a fault stays inside its own pool. Azure's pattern partitions instances by consumer load and availability needs [[tr5]]. For models that means separate deployments or per-consumer limits for batch, interactive and experimental workloads; Azure advises separate deployments because mixed workloads share batches and cache [[r27]]. **Hedging** sends a duplicate after about the 95th-percentile delay and takes the first reply. In a Google BigTable benchmark it cut the 99.9th percentile for 1,000 key reads from 1,800 ms to 74 ms for about 2% extra requests [[r19]] (figures from a search summary, PDF not parsed).

explain.title: Circuit breaker states
explain.alt: Closed moves to open when failures exceed a threshold. Open moves to half-open after the trip duration. Half-open returns to closed if probes succeed or to open if one fails.
explain.src:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Closed
  Closed --> Open: failures exceed threshold
  Open --> HalfOpen: trip duration ends
  HalfOpen --> Closed: probes succeed
  HalfOpen --> Open: a probe fails

explain.caption: Which tool for which failure
head: Failure
Tool
Why
rows: A dependency is down or very slow
Fail fast, give it room to recover
Cap its pool, protect the others
A rare slow call on a cheap, idempotent request

whereToUse: APIM backend pools across two model regions
Separate deployments for batch, interactive and experimental traffic
Per-tool concurrency limits in an agent runtime
Hedged calls to embeddings, reranking or short classification
Dependency calls from retrieval to search, storage or tools

use: Breaker: a dependency can fail for minutes and callers would otherwise pile up
Bulkhead: several workloads with different value share capacity
Hedging: tail latency hurts, the call is cheap, idempotent and short
avoid: Hedging long generations or tool calls with side effects: it doubles spend and risks duplicates
A breaker with a trip duration shorter than the dependency's recovery time
Hedging when the cause is overload: duplicates add load
flips: Provider returns long Retry-After: set `acceptRetryAfter` so the breaker honours it
Hedge rate exceeds a small budget: stop hedging and fix the tail
One tenant dominates traffic: give it a pool of its own

pitfalls.symptom: Callers see 503 with no sign of an outage
pitfalls.cause: The gateway breaker is open and the error is gateway-originated
pitfalls.fix: Tag gateway errors in traces, alert on breaker open time and show it on the dashboard

pitfalls.symptom: The breaker flaps open and closed
pitfalls.cause: Trip duration is short and half-open probes hit a still-sick dependency
pitfalls.fix: Lengthen or back off the trip duration; accept Retry-After for Azure OpenAI backends

pitfalls.symptom: Hedging raised the bill and the error rate
pitfalls.cause: Duplicates were sent for long generations during an overload
pitfalls.fix: Hedge only cheap idempotent calls, cap the hedge rate and cancel the losing request

scenarios.title: A batch job crowds out chat
scenarios.situation: A nightly pipeline and an interactive chat share one deployment. When the pipeline runs, chat users see slow replies and 429s.
constraints: The pipeline can move or shrink
unknowns: Is there a gateway to enforce per-consumer limits?
scenarios.question: Which isolation fits?

options.name: Bulkhead: separate deployments, or per-consumer token limits, and Batch for the pipeline
options.why: The failure is contention, not a dependency outage. Isolating pools protects chat directly.
options.tradeoff: Quota is fragmented and each pool needs headroom.

options.name: A circuit breaker on the pipeline
options.why: Breakers react to failures of a dependency, not to a consumer using too much capacity.
options.tradeoff: Right when the model endpoint itself fails.

options.name: Hedge chat requests
options.why: Duplicates add load to a saturated deployment.
options.tradeoff: Right for a rare slow tail with spare capacity.

flips.if: Only a few teams and low volume
flips.then: A single deployment with a simple limiter may do.
Batch makes the isolation nearly free.

scenarios.takeaway: Contention needs a bulkhead, not a breaker.

scenarios.title: A slow tail on reranking
scenarios.situation: A reranking call is cheap, idempotent and usually answers in 80 ms, but 1 in 100 calls takes over 1 second and blows the retrieval budget.
constraints: Latency budget for retrieval is 400 ms
unknowns: Why is the tail slow: queueing, a cold node or overload?
scenarios.question: What do you apply?

options.name: Hedge after about the p95 delay, with a hedge budget and cancellation
options.why: The call is cheap and idempotent, so an early duplicate trims the tail for a few percent extra requests.
options.tradeoff: Extra load and cost on the hedged calls.

options.name: Retry after a 1 second timeout
options.tradeoff: The user already waited the full timeout.

options.name: Open a circuit breaker on slow responses
options.why: A one-percent tail is not a dependency outage and the breaker would reject healthy traffic.
options.tradeoff: Right for sustained high error or latency.

flips.if: The tail is caused by overload
flips.then: Hedging adds load; fix capacity first.

flips.if: The call is a long generation
flips.then: Do not hedge; use a deadline and fallback.

scenarios.takeaway: Hedge cheap, idempotent calls with spare capacity.

scenarios.title: Primary region keeps failing with long Retry-After
scenarios.situation: The primary region returns 429 and 503 with Retry-After values of many minutes. A secondary region exists behind the gateway.
unknowns: Does the API need session affinity?
scenarios.question: How should the gateway behave?

options.name: Priority pool with a breaker that accepts Retry-After and a warmed secondary
options.why: The breaker stays open for the advertised time and traffic flows to the secondary without client changes.
options.tradeoff: The secondary starts with a cold cache and needs quota.

options.name: Round-robin both regions
options.tradeoff: Keeps sending half the traffic to a failing region.

options.name: Hedge every request across both regions
options.why: It doubles cost and load permanently to mask a regional fault.
options.tradeoff: Right only for rare tail events on cheap calls.

flips.then: Add session affinity or accept losing state on failover.
Fix capacity first, or degrade features.

scenarios.takeaway: A breaker with accepted Retry-After plus a ready secondary fails over cleanly.

quiz.q: Order the life of a circuit breaker after a dependency starts failing.
items: Half-open: a few probe calls pass
quiz.explain: Failures push it open. After the trip duration, half-open allows probes. Success closes it, failure reopens it [[tr4]].

quiz.q: You hedge any request still unanswered after the p95 latency. At most what percentage of requests send a duplicate?
quiz.explain: By definition 5% of requests take longer than p95, so at most about 5% trigger a hedge; cancelling the loser and faster replies can bring it lower, as in the BigTable benchmark's roughly 2% [[r19]]. Derived.

quiz.q: The cause of slowness is overload on the dependency. What does hedging do?
options: Adds load and can worsen the slowdown
quiz.explain: Duplicates add requests to an already saturated service. Hedging suits a slow tail with spare capacity, not overload. It does not cache or trip breakers.

flashcards.back: Closed (count failures), open (reject fast), half-open (probe with a few calls). APIM returns 503 when open.
Partition capacity into pools so one consumer's fault or load stays inside its own pool.
Cheap, idempotent, short calls with spare capacity. Hedge after about p95, cap the hedge rate and cancel the loser.
